chunks: Allah has mercy on him, Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn 'Imran al-Daqqaq narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Kulayni, from Ali ibn Muhammad, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ibrahim ibn Muhammad al-Hamdani, who said:

I wrote to the man, meaning Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him), informing him that those before us from your followers have differed regarding Divine Unity; some of them say [God has] a body, and some of them say [God has] an image. So he (peace be upon him) wrote in his own handwriting: 'Glory be to Him who is not limited, and cannot be described; there is nothing whatsoever like unto Him; He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing' — or he said: 'the All--Seeing'.

key_terms.سُبْحَانَ مَنْ لَا يُحَدُّ: Glory to Him who is not limited
key_terms.لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ: There is nothing whatsoever like unto Him

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia theological understanding of God's attributes regarding body and image?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid* highlights the early theological debate among the Shia community regarding whether God possesses a physical form (jism) or an image (surah). Imam al-Hasan (AS) resolves this by affirming divine transcendence (tanzih), emphasizing that God is beyond spatial limits and human description, thereby rejecting anthropomorphism.
